pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Model each as a graph — what are the nodes and edges, is it directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted? (a) a road map for computing driving distances, (b) 'follows' on a social network, (c) mutual friendship.
expected_points: road map: intersections/cities as nodes, roads as edges, weighted by distance; usually undirected (or directed for one-way streets)
follows: people as nodes, directed unweighted edges — A following B says nothing about B following A
friendship: undirected because the relation is symmetric, which in an implementation means storing both directed edges

questions.prompt: For a sparse graph — say a million nodes, a handful of edges each — compare the adjacency list and the adjacency matrix: memory, 'is there an edge u→v?', and iterating u's neighbors. When does the matrix win?
expected_points: list: O(V + E) memory, edge test O(deg(u)), neighbor iteration O(deg(u)); matrix: O(V^2) memory, edge test O(1), neighbor iteration O(V)
sparse means E is far below V^2, so the matrix wastes almost all its cells — a million nodes means 10^12 cells
the matrix wins only for small or dense graphs, or when O(1) edge tests dominate everything else

questions.prompt: Tree traversals in the previous lessons had no visited set, yet your BFS and DFS require one. Why the difference, and what exactly goes wrong without it?
expected_points: trees guarantee one parent and no cycles, so no node can be reached twice; graphs revoke both guarantees
without visited tracking, a node reachable by two routes is visited more than once
on a cycle the traversal never terminates — BFS's queue never drains, DFS recurses until the stack overflows — so the visited set is what makes traversal terminate, not an optimization

questions.prompt: Why does BFS find shortest paths in an unweighted graph, while DFS does not? And why does the argument break down once edges have weights?
expected_points: the queue makes BFS explore in distance order — all nodes at distance d are discovered before any at d+1 — so the first time a node is reached is via the fewest edges
DFS commits to one branch and reports whatever route it stumbles into first, which may be far longer than the shortest
with weights, fewest edges no longer means cheapest path (two cost-1 hops beat one cost-10 hop), which is where an algorithm like Dijkstra's takes over

questions.prompt: A deploy tool must answer 'does service A transitively depend on service B?' over a directed dependency graph. How do you answer it with what you built, and what does one query cost?
expected_points: traverse from A — BFS or DFS equally, since only the reachable set matters, not the order — and check whether B is visited
cost is O(V + E) with an adjacency list: each node enqueued once, each edge examined once
direction matters: A reaching B says nothing about B reaching A

questions.prompt: For edges added in order 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→5, 4→6: predict the exact BFS and DFS orders from 1, without running the code.
expected_points: BFS: 1 2 3 4 5 6 — whole levels at a time
DFS: 1 2 4 6 3 5 — down the first-neighbor spine, then backtrack to 3
same six nodes either way; only the order differs

questions.prompt: Your ShortestPathLen records dist[neighbor] = dist[node] + 1 at discovery time and never updates it. Why is never updating safe in BFS, when in general a later route could be shorter?
expected_points: BFS discovers nodes in nondecreasing distance order, so at discovery time the recorded distance is already minimal
any later route to the same node comes from a node discovered no earlier, so it can only be as long or longer
this is exactly the property that fails under edge weights, forcing weighted algorithms to revise tentative distances
